bib.title: LiveMCP-101: Stress Testing and Diagnosing MCP-enabled Agents on Challenging Queries

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: All 23 pages read (76,830 chars extracted, clean text). Nothing skimmed except the reference list (names only). Appendix A-D read (plans, failure cases, run stability Table 3, judge cross-check Table 4, judge prompts). No embedded instructions found.

SOURCE: "LiveMCP-101: Stress Testing and Diagnosing MCP-enabled Agents on Challenging Queries". First author Ming Yin (Duke University and Zoom); other authors are mostly Zoom. Corresponding authors Yiran Chen (Duke) and Kaiqiang Song (Zoom). arXiv 2508.15760v2, dated 22 May 2026 in the PDF stamp. No venue is stated, and the header reads "Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size", so treat it as a preprint (ICML-style template).

CORE CLAIM: 101 real-world multi-step tasks over live MCP tools (41 servers, 260 tools) are hard for frontier models. Because live tool answers drift, the grader runs a reference agent on a human-validated plan at the same time as the tested agent and compares the two outputs. That gives a "dynamic ground truth".

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. GPT-5 has the best task success rate (TSR), 58.42% overall. The setup is 18 LLMs (21 rows in Table 2 counting extended-thinking variants), 101 tasks, ReAct, 30-round cap, a per-task pool of 15 MCP servers (76-125 tools), and GPT-4.1 as judge. TSR means a result Likert score of 5, normalized to 1.00. Average result score (ARS) is 73.02%. Next come o3 at 46.53% and GPT-5-mini at 43.56%.
2. Success falls with difficulty (Easy 30, Medium 30, Hard 41 tasks). GPT-5 scores 86.67% Easy, 56.67% Medium and 39.02% Hard. Qwen3-235B-A22B, the best open-source model, scores 22.77% TSR and 42.57% ARS overall, and 4.88% on Hard. Llama-3.1-8B scores 0.99%.
3. Failure mix, as a share of all 101 tasks (Fig 7, single run per model). Semantic parameter errors are the largest failure type: 16.8% for GPT-5 and 41.6% for GPT-4.1-mini. Syntactic errors are 0.0% for GPT-5 but 48.5% for Llama-3.3-70B. There are 7 subtypes: ignoring requirement, overconfident self-solving, unproductive thinking, wrong tool selection, syntactic errors, semantic errors, output parsing errors.
4. Judge reliability: quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa between humans and the LLM judge is above 0.85 on results and above 0.78 on trajectories. The sample is 30 tasks (10 per tier), 6 models, blind experts using the same rubric. Figure 6 values run from 85.1 to 88.2 for results and from 78.4 to 81.5 for trajectories. Swapping the judge (GPT-4.1, Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro) over all 101 tasks gives a TSR SD of 0.57 to 1.14 (Table 4).
5. Run-to-run stability (Table 3): three runs of 6 models. GPT-5 TSR is 58.33, 56.67 and 58.33 (SD 0.96).
6. Round budget (Fig 5): TSR rises from 15 to about 25 rounds, then flattens (tested 15, 20, 25, 30, 50; 6 models). A larger distractor pool (6 to 15 servers) hurts weaker models, while GPT-5 and Claude-4.1-Opus (ET) stay about flat.

QUOTES
- "even frontier LLMs achieve a success rate below 60%" (p1, abstract)
- "unlike subjective rubric-based scoring, the LLM judge verifies the agent's outputs against the reference outputs." (p4, 3.2.2)
- "Semantic errors are the dominant failure." (p8)

METRICS: Beyond TSR and ARS, an average trajectory score (ATS) is the mean of the normalized 1-5 trajectory Likert, as (score-1)/4. Token cost is output tokens summed over rounds, averaged per task. ATS rises with TSR and ARS (Fig 4a). Closed models show a log-shaped TSR-vs-tokens curve, and open models convert tokens to success worse.

LIMITS / NOT SHOWN
- Table 2 and Fig 7 appear to be one run per model. The 3-run check covers only 6 models.
- Table 3 percentages (58.33, 56.67, 43.33, 23.33) are multiples of 1/60, which cannot come from 101 tasks. This is unexplained and the numbers may come from a subset; treat the SD claim with caution. Table 3's GPT-5 run 1 (58.33) differs slightly from Table 2 (58.42).
- The reference agent is GPT-4.1, and the judge is also GPT-4.1. GPT-4.1 judges its own family, and the paper only partly tests this with the cross-judge table. Only 6 models were cross-judged.
- The human-validated plan took about 120 expert-hours. Each task was validated over at least 3 runs, but the plan is only a reference, not the only correct path.
- Tasks are objectively verifiable, so the paper itself says the judge mainly handles formatting. It does not show how the judge fares on open-ended outputs.
- Trajectory scoring is an LLM Likert (kappa 0.78+); there is no step-level match against the plan.
- No stated limitations section. The Impact Statement is generic. The paper makes no cost-in-dollars or latency claims.
- Models are Aug 2025 vintage (GPT-5, Claude-4.1); the rankings have dated.
- Difficulty tiers were set by author consensus, not computed.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022/2023); MCP (Anthropic, 2024); LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) and G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023); Likert scoring; Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960). Benchmarks it compares against: BFCL, tau-bench, ToolSandbox, StableToolBench, MCPWorld, MCP-RADAR, MCPEval, LiveMCPBench (Mo et al., 2025), MCP-Bench (Wang et al., 2025). Its own claim is that those lack real-time, verifiable ground truth.

BEST-FIT NOTE SECTION: "Outcome and trajectory" (lines 68+). It is the one benchmark here that scores both result and trajectory 1-5 and reports ATS tracking TSR. "Scoring tool calls" is the second fit. That section is a match-mode table (exact, in order, any order, subset), and LiveMCP-101 does not match calls; it judges against a live reference output. "Agent-specific suites" holds benchmark case studies (MedBrowseComp, NatureBench) in the same style, so a short paragraph there is also possible. The note currently has no mention of MCP or LiveMCP. It lacks: (a) a live-reference ("dynamic ground truth") pattern for tools whose answers change over time; (b) an error taxonomy for tool use (semantic vs syntactic parameters, overconfident self-solving, output parsing); (c) distractor-pool and round-budget sensitivity.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p1/p2) shows the parallel reference and evaluated agent pipeline into an LLM judge. It explains the core design fastest. Alternative: Figure 7 (p8), the error-type heatmap by model.
